1	# Looking Inside the Compiler: `.i`, `.bc`, and IR
2	
3	A lab built around files you generate and read. The rule for the whole sheet:
4	**don't trust the explanation — generate the file and look.**
5	
6	## The pipeline map (keep this in front of you)
7	
8	`clang` is not a single program. It is a *driver* that runs a chain of tools,
9	and each tool hands a file to the next:
10	
11	```
12	 file.c
13	   │  preprocessor        clang -E
14	   ▼
15	 file.i      ← preprocessed C: still text, all #includes pasted in
16	   │  clang front-end     (parse  →  generate LLVM IR)
17	   ▼
18	 IR  (.ll text / .bc binary)   ← the same program, now in LLVM's language
19	   │  LLVM back-end       clang -S
20	   ▼
21	 file.s      ← native assembly for this CPU
22	   │  assembler           clang -c
23	   ▼
24	 file.o      ← machine code, not yet linked
25	   │  linker
26	   ▼
27	 a.out       ← executable
28	```
29	
30	The single most important idea on this sheet: **clang always passes through
31	LLVM IR.** It never turns C straight into assembly. The `.ll`/`.bc` files just
32	let you *see* a step that is always happening.
33	
34	To dump every stage at once:
35	
36	```
37	clang --save-temps -c file.c
38	```
39	
40	---
41	
42	# Concept 1 — `#include` is literal text insertion
43	
44	### a. What we set up / save in a file
45	
46	Run *only* the preprocessor and save its output as a `.i` file:
47	
48	```
49	clang -E hello.c -o hello.i
50	```
51	
52	`-E` = "stop after preprocessing." The `.i` file is the exact text the rest of
53	the compiler will actually see. Nothing in it knows the word `#include` anymore.
54	
55	Example files to create:
56	
57	```c
58	/* hello.c */
59	#include <stdio.h>
60	int main()
61	{
62	    printf("Hello\n");
63	    return 0;
64	}
65	```
66	
67	```c
68	/* util.h */
69	int add(int a, int b);
70	
71	/* use.c */
72	#include "util.h"
73	int main() { return add(1, 2); }
74	```
75	
76	```c
77	/* bare.c  — no includes at all */
78	int main() { return 0; }
79	```
80	
81	### b. Task
82	
83	1. For each file, generate the `.i` and compare sizes:
84	   ```
85	   clang -E hello.c -o hello.i
86	   wc -l hello.c hello.i
87	   ```
88	   **Note:** `wc` command is used to count words. Check it's man page using `man wc` command. Check about the option `-l` in it's man page.
89	2. Do the same for `use.c` and `bare.c`. Line up the three before/after counts.
90	3. In `hello.i`, find the line where `printf` is actually declared:
91	   ```
92	   grep -n "int printf" hello.i
93	   ```
94	4. In `use.i`, find the line you wrote in `util.h`:
95	   ```
96	   grep -n "int add" use.i
97	   ```
98	5. Open `bare.i` and read the *whole* thing.
99	
100	### c. Observation (what you should find)
101	
102	- `hello.c` is ~7 lines; `hello.i` is **several hundred** (on a typical Linux
103	  box, well over 800). One `#include <stdio.h>` dragged in the entire contents
104	  of `stdio.h` *and every header stdio.h itself includes*.
105	- The declaration `extern int printf(...)` is physically sitting inside
106	  `hello.i` — it was copied there from the system header. Your program didn't
107	  "import" printf; the text of its declaration was pasted in.
108	- The line `int add(int a, int b);` you wrote in `util.h` appears verbatim near
109	  the top of `use.i`. `#include "util.h"` did nothing more clever than copy-paste.
110	- `bare.i` has almost nothing in it — proof that the bulk of `hello.i` came
111	  *entirely* from the `#include`, not from your code.
112	
113	**Takeaway to say out loud:** `#include` is a copy-paste of one file's text into
114	another, performed before the compiler runs. That is the whole feature.
115	
116	---
117	
118	# Concept 2 — How error messages still point at *your* line
119	
120	This is the question "if the compiler only ever sees the `.i` file, how does it
121	report errors against `hello.c` line 5?"
122	
123	### a. What we set up / save in a file
124	
125	Look at the top of any `.i` file. Mixed in with the code are lines like:
126	
127	```
128	# 1 "hello.c"
129	# 1 "<built-in>" 1
130	# 1 "hello.c" 2
131	# 1 "/usr/include/stdio.h" 1 3 4
132	```
133	
134	These are **line markers** (the preprocessor writes them into the `.i`). Format:
135	
136	```
137	# <line-number> "<file-name>" <flags>
138	```
139	
140	A marker means: *"the text that follows is line `<line-number>` of
141	`<file-name>`."* The compiler reads each marker and resets its internal
142	line counter and current-file name. That is the entire mechanism that maps the
143	giant `.i` back onto your small `.c`.
144	
145	The flags (optional) are hints:
146	
147	| flag | meaning                                         |
148	|------|-------------------------------------------------|
149	| `1`  | we just **entered** a new file (an `#include`)  |
150	| `2`  | we just **returned** to a file (include ended)  |
151	| `3`  | text is from a **system header** (mutes warnings) |
152	| `4`  | treat as implicit `extern "C"`                  |
153	
154	### b. Task
155	
156	1. Put a deliberate bug in `hello.c` — delete the semicolon after the `printf`
157	   call. Compile it and note the reported location:
158	   ```
159	   clang -c hello.c
160	   ```
161	2. Now preprocess *first*, then compile the `.i`, and see where it claims the
162	   error is:
163	   ```
164	   clang -E hello.c -o hello.i
165	   grep -n "printf" hello.i        # note the PHYSICAL line in hello.i
166	   clang -c hello.i
167	   ```
168	  **Note:** `grep` command is used to search. Check it's man page using `man grep` command. Check about the option `-n` it's man page.
169	  
170	3. Find the last `# N "hello.c" 2` marker in `hello.i` (the one just before
171	   `main`). Edit it by hand — change it to `# 100 "AIK.c"`. Recompile the
172	   edited `.i` and read the error location.
173	
174	### c. Observation (what you should find)
175	
176	- In step 1 the error is reported at, e.g., `hello.c:5:...`.
177	- In step 2 the `printf` call physically lives on line ~831 of `hello.i`, yet the
178	  error message **still says `hello.c:5`** — not line 831. The compiler used the
179	  line markers to translate the position back.
180	- In step 3, after you lie in the marker, the compiler *believes you*: the error
181	  now reads something like `AIK.c:103:...`. Count the physical lines from your
182	  faked `# 100 "AIK.c"` marker down to the bug and you'll see the number lines
183	  up exactly. The compiler trusts the marker completely.
184	
185	**Takeaway to say out loud:** the preprocessor plants signposts
186	(`# line "file"`) all through the `.i`, each one announcing "you are here." Error
187	line numbers are not magic — they are the compiler reading the nearest signpost.
188	
189	---
190	
191	# Concept 3 — The `.bc` file: when it appears and what's in it
192	
193	### a. What we set up / save in a file
194	
195	Dump every intermediate at once and list what you got:
196	
197	```
198	clang --save-temps -c square.c
199	ls -l square.*
200	```
201	
202	You will see `square.i`, `square.bc`, `square.s`, `square.o`. The `.bc` sits
203	**after `.i` and before `.s`** in the chain — exactly the "IR" box in the
204	pipeline map. `.bc` stands for **bitcode**: the *binary* serialized form of LLVM
205	IR. It is the same information as the `.ll` text file in Concept 4, just packed
206	into bytes for tools to read quickly.
207	
208	Example file:
209	
210	```c
211	/* square.c */
212	int square(int n) { return n * n; }
213	```
214	
215	### b. Task
216	
217	1. Run `--save-temps` on `square.c` and on `hello.c`. List the products of each
218	   and place them in pipeline order yourself.
219	2. Confirm `.bc` is binary, not text:
220	   ```
221	   file square.bc
222	   od -A d -t x1 square.bc | head -1
223	   ```
224	3. Turn the binary bitcode back into readable text to prove they are the same
225	   thing (the tool may be named `llvm-dis` or `llvm-dis-18`):
226	   ```
227	   llvm-dis square.bc -o square_from_bc.ll
228	   cat square_from_bc.ll
229	   ```
230	  **Note:** Command `llvm-dis` is used to **dis**assemble llvm bitcode. Command `file` determines file type. Check man pages for each command using `man llvm-dis` and `man file`. 
231	
232	### c. Observation (what you should find)
233	
234	- `--save-temps` produces `.i .bc .s .o` — the `.bc` confirms IR really is a
235	  stage clang passes through, between preprocessed source and assembly.
236	- `file` reports `LLVM IR bitcode`, and the first bytes are
237	  `42 43 c0 de` — ASCII `B`, `C`, then `0xC0 0xDE`. That four-byte "magic number"
238	  (`BC\xC0\xDE`) is how tools recognize a bitcode file. You cannot read it in a
239	  text editor.
240	- `llvm-dis` turns `square.bc` back into perfectly readable IR — identical in
241	  content to what you'll see in Concept 4. So `.bc` is not a *different* thing
242	  from IR; it is IR written in binary instead of text.
243	
244	**Takeaway to say out loud:** `.bc` is generated right after preprocessing,
245	before assembly. It contains LLVM IR in binary form — the compiler's internal
246	representation of your program, frozen to disk.
247	
248	---
249	
250	# Concept 4 — IR code: when it's generated and how to read it
251	
252	### a. What we set up / save in a file
253	
254	IR (LLVM Intermediate Representation) is generated by the clang **front-end**,
255	straight after it parses the preprocessed `.i`. You can ask clang to stop and
256	hand it to you in either form:
257	
258	```
259	clang -emit-llvm -S square.c -o square.ll     # .ll = TEXT IR (human-readable)
260	clang -emit-llvm -c square.c -o square.bc      # .bc = BINARY IR (bitcode)
261	```
262	
263	`-emit-llvm` means "produce LLVM IR instead of native assembly." Pair it with
264	`-S` for text, `-c` for binary. `.ll` and `.bc` are the same content in two
265	encodings (Concept 3 already showed you can convert between them).
266	
267	### b. Task
268	
269	1. Generate `square.ll` and read it. Identify: the function signature, where the
270	   argument is stored, where the multiply happens, where it returns.
271	2. Generate IR for `hello.c` too and skim it — notice the `call` to `printf` and
272	   the string constant.
273	3. Watch the optimizer rewrite the IR. Generate it once unoptimized and once
274	   optimized, then compare:
275	   ```
276	   clang -O0 -emit-llvm -S square.c -o sq_O0.ll
277	   clang -O2 -emit-llvm -S square.c -o sq_O2.ll
278	   diff sq_O0.ll sq_O2.ll
279	   ```
280	4. Confirm IR really does sit *before* assembly: generate `square.s`
281	   (`clang -S square.c`) and eyeball that the `.s` is plainly a translation of
282	   the IR you just read, not of the C directly.
283	
284	### c. Observation (what you should find)
285	
286	- The `-O0` IR for `square` is wordy and literal — it allocates a stack slot,
287	  *stores* the argument, *loads* it back **twice**, multiplies, returns. It
288	  mirrors the naïve meaning of the C with nothing cleaned up:
289	  ```
290	  %2 = alloca i32
291	  store i32 %0, ptr %2
292	  %3 = load i32, ptr %2
293	  %4 = load i32, ptr %2
294	  %5 = mul nsw i32 %3, %4
295	  ret i32 %5
296	  ```
297	- The `-O2` IR collapses to the essence — no stack traffic at all:
298	  ```
299	  %2 = mul nsw i32 %0, %0
300	  ret i32 %2
301	  ```
302	  The `diff` makes the optimizer's work visible: it proved the loads/stores were
303	  pointless and deleted them.
304	- The IR is clearly *between* C and assembly: it still has named, typed values
305	  (`i32`) and a `mul` instruction (more abstract than machine code), but it is
306	  already in straight-line, one-operation-per-line form (lower-level than C).
307	- Reading `square.s` afterwards, the assembly is recognizably a translation of
308	  the IR — confirming the real path is **C → IR → assembly**, never C → assembly.
309	
310	**Takeaway to say out loud:** IR is the compiler's own language, produced right
311	after parsing. `.ll` is its text form, `.bc` its binary form. Everything the
312	optimizer does, it does to the IR — which is why reading IR is the clearest
313	window into *what the compiler decided to do with your code.*
314	
315	---
316	
317	## One-page command reference
318	
319	| Goal                                  | Command                                  |
320	|---------------------------------------|------------------------------------------|
321	| Preprocessed source only (`.i`)       | `clang -E file.c -o file.i`              |
322	| Preprocessed, no line markers         | `clang -E -P file.c`                     |
323	| All intermediates (`.i .bc .s .o`)    | `clang --save-temps -c file.c`           |
324	| Text IR (`.ll`)                       | `clang -emit-llvm -S file.c -o file.ll`  |
325	| Binary IR / bitcode (`.bc`)           | `clang -emit-llvm -c file.c -o file.bc`  |
326	| Bitcode → readable text               | `llvm-dis file.bc -o file.ll`            |
327	| Native assembly (`.s`)                | `clang -S file.c`                        |
328	| Compare optimizer effect on IR        | `clang -O0/-O2 -emit-llvm -S file.c`     |
329	
330	**Order to remember:** `.c → .i → IR (.ll/.bc) → .s → .o → executable`.
331	
332	---
333	
334	## New Words (కొత్త పదాలు — తెలుగు అర్థాలు)
335	
336	| English word | తెలుగు అర్థం |
337	|--------------|--------------|
338	| **signpost** | మార్గసూచిక / దారిచూపే బోర్డు — "మీరు ఇక్కడ ఉన్నారు" అని చూపే బోర్డు. ఇక్కడ line marker లను దీనితో పోల్చాం. |
339	| **preprocessor** | ముందస్తు ప్రాసెసర్ — కంపైలర్ నడవడానికి *ముందు* నడిచే దశ. ఇది C భాష అర్థం చేసుకోదు, కేవలం పాఠ్యాన్ని (text) మాత్రమే మారుస్తుంది. |
340	| **compiler** | కంపైలర్ (సంకలని) — మనం రాసిన C ప్రోగ్రామ్‌ను యంత్ర భాషలోకి అనువదించే సాధనం. |
341	| **driver** | డ్రైవర్ — అనేక చిన్న సాధనాలను వరుసగా నడిపించే ప్రధాన కార్యక్రమం (clang ఒక డ్రైవర్). |
342	| **intermediate file** | మధ్యంతర ఫైల్ — తుది ఫలితానికి ముందు, ప్రతి దశలో తయారయ్యే మధ్యలోని ఫైల్. |
343	| **preprocessed source** (`.i`) | ముందస్తుగా ప్రాసెస్ చేయబడిన కోడ్ — అన్ని `#include`లు చేర్చబడిన తర్వాత మిగిలే పాఠ్య రూపంలోని C కోడ్. |
344	| **header file** | హెడర్ ఫైల్ — ప్రకటనలు (declarations) ఉండే ఫైల్; `#include` ద్వారా చేర్చబడుతుంది. |
345	| **declaration** | ప్రకటన — ఒక ఫంక్షన్ లేదా చరరాశి ఉనికిని తెలిపే వాక్యం. |
346	| **text insertion** | పాఠ్య చొప్పింపు — ఒక ఫైల్ యొక్క పాఠ్యాన్ని మరో ఫైల్‌లో నేరుగా కాపీ-పేస్ట్ చేయడం. |
347	| **line marker** | పంక్తి గుర్తు — `.i` ఫైల్‌లో `# 5 "hello.c"` లాంటి గుర్తు; "ఈ క్రింది పాఠ్యం hello.c లోని 5వ పంక్తి" అని చెబుతుంది. |
348	| **flag** | సూచిక / ఫ్లాగ్ — అదనపు సమాచారం ఇచ్చే చిన్న గుర్తు (1, 2, 3, 4). |
349	| **system header** | సిస్టమ్ హెడర్ — ఆపరేటింగ్ సిస్టమ్/లైబ్రరీతో పాటు వచ్చే సిద్ధ హెడర్ ఫైళ్ళు (ఉదా: `stdio.h`). |
350	| **IR / Intermediate Representation** | మధ్యంతర ప్రాతినిధ్యం — C కి, యంత్ర భాషకి మధ్యలో ఉండే LLVM యొక్క సొంత భాష. |
351	| **bitcode** (`.bc`) | బిట్‌కోడ్ — IR యొక్క ద్విआధార (binary) రూపం; మనుషులు చదవలేరు, సాధనాలు మాత్రమే చదవగలవు. |
352	| **binary** | ద్విआధార (బైనరీ) — 0లు, 1లతో కూడిన, మనుషులు నేరుగా చదవలేని రూపం. |
353	| **magic number** | మ్యాజిక్ నంబర్ — ఫైల్ రకాన్ని గుర్తించడానికి ఫైల్ మొదట్లో ఉండే ప్రత్యేక బైట్లు (`BC\xC0\xDE`). |
354	| **assembly** | అసెంబ్లీ — ఒక నిర్దిష్ట CPU కోసం తయారైన తక్కువ-స్థాయి (low-level) భాష. |
355	| **assembler** | అసెంబ్లర్ — అసెంబ్లీని యంత్ర కోడ్ (`.o`)గా మార్చే సాధనం. |
356	| **linker** | లింకర్ — అనేక `.o` ఫైళ్ళను, లైబ్రరీలను కలిపి ఒక executable తయారుచేసే సాధనం. |
357	| **executable** | నిర్వహించదగిన ఫైల్ — నేరుగా నడిపించగల తుది ప్రోగ్రామ్ (ఉదా: `a.out`). |

# Debugging C Code Using Clang Debugger (LLDB) — Level-1

A lab built around *watching your program run one line at a time*. The rule for
the whole sheet: **don't guess what the code does — stop it, step it, and look
at the variables.**

All commands are for the **Ubuntu shell**. The debugger we use is **LLDB**, the
debugger that comes from the same project as `clang`.

## What is debugging?

When a program gives a wrong answer, the bug is somewhere in the lines you
wrote — but *which* line? Reading the code again and again is guessing.
A **debugger** removes the guessing: it runs your program in slow motion,
**pausing before every line**, and lets you ask *"what is inside each variable
right now?"*

Think of it like watching a cricket replay frame by frame instead of at full
speed — you see exactly the moment things went wrong.

## The debug loop map (keep this in front of you)

```
 write main.c
   │
   ▼
 clang -g main.c -o main      ← compile WITH the -g flag (debug info)
   │
   ▼
 lldb ./main                  ← start the debugger, program NOT running yet
   │
   ▼
 b main                       ← set a breakpoint at the start of main
   │
   ▼
 run                          ← program starts, then FREEZES at main
   │
   ▼
 next  →  next  →  next ...   ← execute ONE line at a time (step-over)
   │        (after every next: frame variable — look at the values)
   ▼
 program ends → quit          ← leave the debugger
```

One rule for this whole task: we only use **`next`** (step-over). LLDB also has
`step` (step-in) and `finish` (step-out) — those only matter once your programs
have *functions other than `main`*. We will meet them in **Level-2**, after you
learn to write your own functions.

## Setup (one time)

Check that both tools exist:

```
clang --version
lldb --version
```

If either is missing, install them:

```
sudo apt update
sudo apt install clang lldb
```

---

# Concept 1 — The `-g` flag: giving the debugger a map

### a. What we set up / save in a file

A compiled executable is machine code — it has no idea what `int a` or
"line 7" means. The `-g` flag tells clang to pack **debug information** into
the executable: which machine instruction came from which source line, and
where each variable lives. Without `-g`, LLDB is blind.

Create this file:

```c
/* biggest.c */
#include <stdio.h>

int main()
{
    int a = 7;
    int b = 12;
    int big = a;

    if (b > big)
    {
        big = b;
    }

    printf("biggest = %d\n", big);
    return 0;
}
```

Compile it **twice** — once without `-g`, once with:

```
clang biggest.c -o biggest_blind
clang -g biggest.c -o biggest
```

### b. Task

1. Compare the sizes of the two executables:
   ```
   ls -l biggest_blind biggest
   ```
2. Ask `file` what it thinks of each one:
   ```
   file biggest_blind biggest
   ```
   **Note:** `file` determines a file's type. Check its man page using
   `man file`.
3. Run both programs normally — confirm they behave *identically*:
   ```
   ./biggest_blind
   ./biggest
   ```

### c. Observation (what you should find)

- `biggest` (built with `-g`) is **bigger** than `biggest_blind` — the extra
  bytes are the debug information, the "map" from machine code back to your
  `.c` lines and variable names.
- `file` reports the `-g` version as `with debug_info, not stripped`.
- Both print `biggest = 12`. Debug info changes **nothing** about what the
  program does — it is baggage for the debugger, invisible during a normal run.

**Takeaway to say out loud:** `-g` doesn't change the program; it packs a map
into the executable so the debugger can point at *your* source lines and *your*
variable names. **Always compile with `-g` before debugging.**

---

# Concept 2 — Starting LLDB and freezing the program at `main`

### a. What we set up / save in a file

Start the debugger with your program:

```
lldb ./biggest
```

The shell prompt changes to `(lldb)` — you are now talking to the debugger,
not the shell. **Important: your program has not started yet.** LLDB has only
loaded it, like an arrow placed on the bow but not released.

A **breakpoint** is a marker meaning *"when the running program reaches this
place, freeze."* We put one at the start of `main`:

```
(lldb) breakpoint set --name main
```

Everyone uses the short form:

```
(lldb) b main
```

### b. Task

1. Start LLDB with `./biggest` and set a breakpoint at `main` using `b main`.
2. Confirm the breakpoint exists:
   ```
   (lldb) breakpoint list
   ```
3. Now release the arrow:
   ```
   (lldb) run
   ```
4. Read the screen slowly. Find: the reason it stopped, the file name, the
   line number, and the small arrow `->` in the source listing.
5. Quit and start again — practice the cycle once more:
   ```
   (lldb) quit
   ```
   (LLDB may ask *"Do you really want to proceed"* if the program is still
   frozen mid-run — answer `Y`.)

### c. Observation (what you should find)

- After `run`, LLDB prints something like:
  ```
  Process 4821 stopped
  * thread #1, name = 'biggest', stop reason = breakpoint 1.1
      frame #0: ... main at biggest.c:6
     3    int main()
     4    {
  -> 6        int a = 7;
     7        int b = 12;
  ```
- `stop reason = breakpoint 1.1` — it froze because of *your* breakpoint,
  not a crash.
- The arrow `->` points at `int a = 7;`. Read this carefully: the arrow marks
  the line that is **about to run, and has NOT run yet**. The program is frozen
  *before* line 6, not after it.

**Takeaway to say out loud:** `lldb ./program` loads but does not start;
`b main` plants the freeze-point; `run` starts the program, which immediately
freezes at the first line of `main`. The `->` arrow always means "next line to
execute."

---

# Concept 3 — `next` and `frame variable`: one line at a time, eyes on the variables

### a. What we set up / save in a file

Two commands do almost all Level-1 debugging:

| Command | Short | Meaning |
|---------|-------|---------|
| `next` | `n` | Execute exactly the ONE line at the arrow, then freeze again (**step-over**) |
| `frame variable` | `v` | Show **every local variable** and its current value |
| `print big` | `p big` | Show **one** variable's current value |

The rhythm of debugging is a loop you do with your hands:

```
look at the arrow  →  frame variable  →  next  →  (repeat)
```

We keep using `biggest.c` from Concept 1 — it has an `if`.

### b. Task

1. Start fresh: `lldb ./biggest`, then `b main`, then `run`.
2. Before pressing anything else, look at the variables:
   ```
   (lldb) frame variable
   ```
   Write down the values of `a`, `b`, `big` — yes, *before* any line has run.
3. Now do the rhythm. After **every** `next`, run `frame variable` and note
   which value changed:
   ```
   (lldb) next
   (lldb) frame variable
   ```
   **Note:** pressing plain **Enter** at the `(lldb)` prompt repeats the
   previous command — so you can hammer Enter to keep stepping.
4. When the arrow reaches the `if (b > big)` line, **stop and predict**:
   will the arrow jump *into* the `{ }` block or *over* it? Then press `next`
   once and check.
5. Keep stepping until the program prints `biggest = 12` and exits. Then `quit`.

### c. Observation (what you should find)

- In step 2, **before** `int a = 7;` has run, `frame variable` shows `a`, `b`,
  `big` holding **garbage** — random leftover numbers like `32767` or
  `-1899491328`. A variable has no meaningful value until its line *executes*.
  You are looking at raw memory as it happened to be.
- Each `next` changes exactly **one** thing: after stepping over line 6,
  `a` becomes `7` (while `b`, `big` are still garbage); after line 7,
  `b` becomes `12`; after line 8, `big` becomes `7`.
- At the `if`: since `b (12) > big (7)` is true, the arrow moves **into** the
  block, onto `big = b;`. One more `next` and `frame variable` shows `big`
  jumping from `7` to `12`. You just *watched* an `if` decide.
- Change the experiment: edit `int b = 3;`, recompile with `-g`, and step
  again — this time the arrow **skips the block entirely** and lands straight
  on the `printf` line. The `if` chose the other path, and you saw it.
- On the `printf` line, `next` runs the *whole* printf (that's why it is called
  step-**over**) and `biggest = 12` appears in the middle of your LLDB session.

**Takeaway to say out loud:** `next` executes exactly one of *your* lines;
`frame variable` is the X-ray you take after every step. Watching the arrow at
an `if` shows you the *actual decision*, not the one you assumed.

---

# Concept 4 — Tracing a `while` loop: watch the variables cycle

### a. What we set up / save in a file

Loops are where eyes-only debugging fails — the same lines run again and again
with *different* values. The debugger shows every lap. Create this file:

```c
/* countdown.c */
#include <stdio.h>

int main()
{
    int n = 5;
    int total = 0;

    while (n > 0)
    {
        total = total + n;
        n = n - 1;
    }

    printf("total = %d\n", total);
    return 0;
}
```

Compile with debug info and load it:

```
clang -g countdown.c -o countdown
lldb ./countdown
```

### b. Task

1. `b main`, then `run`.
2. Step with `next` until the arrow first reaches `while (n > 0)`. Check
   `frame variable` — write down `n` and `total`.
3. Keep the rhythm going (`next`, then `frame variable`) around the loop.
   On paper, fill a **trace table** — one row every time the arrow lands on
   the `while` line:

   | lap | `n` when at `while` | `total` when at `while` | will it enter the loop? |
   |-----|--------------------|--------------------------|-------------------------|
   | 1   | 5                  | 0                        | yes / no                |
   | 2   |                    |                          |                         |
   | 3   |                    |                          |                         |
   | ... |                    |                          |                         |

4. **Before each lap**, predict the two values, *then* look. Prediction first,
   `frame variable` second.
5. The important moment: the lap where `n` is `0`. Predict where the arrow will
   go when you press `next` on the `while` line. Then look.
6. If you stepped too far and just want the program to finish normally:
   ```
   (lldb) continue
   ```
   **Note:** `continue` (short `c`) means "stop stepping — run at full speed
   until the next breakpoint or the end."
7. Type `help next` at the `(lldb)` prompt and skim what it says. Every LLDB
   command documents itself this way.

### c. Observation (what you should find)

- The arrow cycles: `while` → `total = total + n;` → `n = n - 1;` → back to
  `while`. The *same three lines*, visited again and again — a loop made
  visible.
- Your trace table fills up as: `n = 5, total = 0` → `n = 4, total = 5` →
  `n = 3, total = 9` → `n = 2, total = 12` → `n = 1, total = 14` →
  `n = 0, total = 15`.
- On the lap where `n` is `0`, the condition `n > 0` is false — `next` makes
  the arrow **jump past the `}` straight to the `printf` line**. That jump *is*
  the loop ending; you watched the exact moment.
- `continue` lets the rest of the program fly by at full speed —
  `total = 15` prints and the process exits.

**Takeaway to say out loud:** a loop is just the arrow travelling in a circle
while the variables change each lap. The trace table you filled by hand *is*
what the debugger shows for free — and when a loop misbehaves (runs forever,
runs one time too many), this is exactly how you catch it.

---

## One-page command reference

| Goal                                   | Command                        | Short |
|----------------------------------------|--------------------------------|-------|
| Compile with debug info                | `clang -g file.c -o file`      | —     |
| Start the debugger                     | `lldb ./file`                  | —     |
| Set breakpoint at start of `main`      | `breakpoint set --name main`   | `b main` |
| List all breakpoints                   | `breakpoint list`              | `br list` |
| Start the program (freezes at breakpoint) | `run`                       | `r`   |
| Execute one line, step-over            | `next`                         | `n`   |
| Show all local variables               | `frame variable`               | `v`   |
| Show one variable                      | `print total`                  | `p total` |
| Run at full speed until next stop      | `continue`                     | `c`   |
| Repeat the previous command            | *(just press Enter)*           | —     |
| Help on any command                    | `help next`                    | —     |
| Leave the debugger                     | `quit`                         | `q`   |

**The Level-1 rhythm to remember:** `b main` → `run` → (`next` → `frame variable`) × many → `continue` → `quit`.

**Coming in Level-2** (after you learn to write functions): `step` (step-in)
and `finish` (step-out) — how to dive into a function call and climb back out.

---

## New Words (కొత్త పదాలు — తెలుగు అర్థాలు)

| English word | తెలుగు అర్థం |
|--------------|--------------|
| **debugging** | దోష నివారణ — ప్రోగ్రామ్‌లో దాగిన తప్పు (bug)ను వెతికి, సరిచేసే ప్రక్రియ. |
| **debugger** | డీబగ్గర్ — ప్రోగ్రామ్‌ను నెమ్మదిగా, పంక్తి-పంక్తిగా నడిపిస్తూ లోపలి విలువలను చూపించే సాధనం (ఇక్కడ LLDB). |

| **debug information** (`-g`) | డీబగ్ సమాచారం — ఏ యంత్ర సూచన ఏ C పంక్తి నుండి వచ్చిందో, ఏ చరరాశి ఎక్కడ ఉందో చెప్పే "మ్యాప్"; `-g` ఫ్లాగ్ దీన్ని executable లో చేరుస్తుంది. |
| **breakpoint** | విరామ బిందువు — "ప్రోగ్రామ్ ఇక్కడికి చేరగానే ఆగిపో" అని పెట్టే గుర్తు. |

# Questions from the class (Q & A)

Real questions students asked while doing this task — read all three even if
you didn't hit them yourself. They are the *same* misunderstanding seen from
three sides.

## Q1. I removed a semicolon at the end of a C statement. Now I can't debug — I just see an error. Why?

**Short answer:** the debugger does not debug your `.c` file — it debugs the
**executable**. Removing the semicolon made the compile *fail*, so no
executable was produced, so there is nothing for LLDB to debug.

Remember what each tool works on:

- `clang` reads your **source code** (`biggest.c`).
- `lldb` reads your **executable** (`./biggest`).

A missing semicolon is a **syntax error**. The compiler refuses to translate a
program it cannot fully understand — it prints the error (something like
`error: expected ';' after expression`) and, crucially, **writes no output
file**. The debugger is downstream of the compiler; a failed compile means the
debugger's input was never created:

```
 THE GATE: only compiled programs can be debugged

 biggest.c ──► clang -g ──✗ error: expected ';'
                 │
                 ▼
          NO executable written
                 │
                 ▼
          nothing for lldb to load  →  cannot debug


 biggest.c ──► clang -g ──✓ compiles clean ──► ./biggest ──► lldb ./biggest ✓
```

**Takeaway to say out loud:** debugging is for programs that *compile but
behave wrongly*. Compile errors are fixed with the **compiler's** message, in
the editor — the debugger only enters the story after `clang -g` succeeds.

## Q2. Strange — I also got a compile error, but I *am* able to debug. How?

**Short answer:** you are debugging a **ghost** — the *old* executable from
your last *successful* compile. The failed compile wrote nothing, but it also
**deleted nothing**, so the old `./biggest` is still sitting on disk and LLDB
happily loads it.

Follow the timeline:

```
 TIME ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────►

 10:00   clang -g biggest.c -o biggest        ✓ success
            └─► writes ./biggest        (a frozen copy of 10:00 code)

 10:05   you edit biggest.c — remove the semicolon

 10:06   clang -g biggest.c -o biggest        ✗ error: expected ';'
            └─► writes NOTHING        (./biggest from 10:00 untouched)

 10:07   lldb ./biggest                        "works"!
            └─► but it is stepping through the 10:00 program,
                NOT the code you are looking at in your editor
```

This is called a **stale executable**, and it is genuinely dangerous: the
source file on your screen and the program under the debugger are *two
different programs*. You will step through lines that "don't match" and see
values that make no sense — and waste an hour doubting yourself.

Two habits prevent it:

1. **Read the compiler's output every single time.** If you saw `error:`, the
   executable was NOT rebuilt — do not touch the debugger until it compiles
   clean.
2. When in doubt, compare timestamps — the executable must be **newer** than
   the source:
   ```
   ls -l biggest.c biggest
   ```
   If `biggest.c` has a later time than `biggest`, the executable is stale.
   (Paranoid version: `rm biggest` before recompiling — then a failed compile
   leaves *nothing* to debug, and Q1's clean error protects you.)

**Takeaway to say out loud:** a failed compile does not erase the previous
executable. LLDB debugs whatever file you hand it — it cannot know your source
has moved on.

## Q3. What is the `lldb` executable?

**Short answer:** `lldb` is itself an ordinary **program** — an executable
file installed on your Ubuntu machine (by `sudo apt install lldb`), exactly as
real as the `./biggest` you built. Its special talent: **its job is to run
*other* programs in slow motion.**

Prove it is just a file on disk, with the tools you already know:

```
which lldb          # where does the shell find it?  e.g. /usr/bin/lldb
file $(which lldb)  # what kind of file is it?       an executable (ELF)
ls -l $(which lldb) # how big? who owns it?
```

So when you type `lldb ./biggest` and press Enter, **two programs** come into
the picture:

```
   you type: b main, run, next, frame variable ...
        │
        ▼
 ┌───────────────────────┐    controls: start, freeze,
 │   lldb                │    step one line, read memory
 │   (the debugger,      │ ─────────────────────────────► ┌──────────────────────┐
 │    a running process) │                                │   ./biggest          │
 │                       │ ◄───────────────────────────── │   (YOUR program,     │
 └───────────────────────┘    reports back: "stopped at   │    a second process) │
                              line 6", "num1 = 7", ...    └──────────────────────┘
```

- **lldb is the puppeteer process.** It shows you the `(lldb)` prompt and
  obeys your commands.
- **Your program is a separate process** (that is the `Process 4821 stopped`
  line!). It is started, frozen, and stepped by lldb — with the operating
  system's permission, since one process controlling another is a privilege
  the OS must grant.
- This is why `quit` sometimes asks *"Do you really want to proceed?"* —
  quitting the puppeteer means abandoning the still-frozen puppet, and lldb
  checks you meant it.

**Takeaway to say out loud:** there is no magic layer — the debugger is a
program like any other. `clang` is a program that *translates* programs;
`lldb` is a program that *runs and controls* programs. You now use programs to
build and inspect programs — that is the whole craft.
EOF
